PRESIDENT’S COLUMN:
Bruce Campbell

May’s Main Event: Laura Fresen of the Wood Co-op on Marketing
Kerry Deane-Cloutier
Laura gave an insightful talk on how to market you turnings. She started with a discussion on the advantages and
disadvantages of representing yourself versus being represented by a gallery or agent. Being represented works for
those who are “make things” people. Being self-represented means you should enjoy sales, and be good at it. You
will be in contact with the public at your points of sale, whether they are trade shows, craft fairs or sales from your
shop.
Her talk focused on being represented. She recommended choosing a number of venues. Most galleries take work
on consignment, and rates of 35-50% are typical in our area. The advantage of consignment is that you set your
own prices, have more flexibility regarding what you make and how much work you provide, and you can remove
your work.
When choosing a gallery, she recommends visiting them. Look at the prices and quality of the items they have.
They should be comparable to yours. Eavesdrop on the customers and staff.
You should consider whether their commission is justified. You should expect sales, and fair exposure in the gallery, perhaps by the work being cycled through the gallery. Make sure that there is a contract between you and the
gallery. It should include terms on who places what insurance, who is responsible for the delivery of work, when
you get paid, and the payment of GST to you. Always track your own inventory.
In turn, the gallery has expectations and guidelines, which they will expect you to follow. These will include
guidelines on consistency in quality and quantity of work, and on pricing (no dumping elsewhere). They will want
you to keep current with trends, but also to keep making items that sell well.
Each gallery will have application procedures for getting in. It is very important to follow them exactly. The review panel may be looking at 40 or 50 at one time, and may toss yours aside if you fail to provide what they want.
Organize your work chronologically, focus most on the work you want to sell, and keep it clean and simple – less
is definitely more here. More generally, a gallery will want to see good design, functionality (the piece does what
it is supposed to do), quality, uniqueness and appropriate pricing.
On improving sales, Laura suggested
•
numbering the work if it is one of a series
•
providing an artist’s statement
•
making limited editions ( e.g. 3 of 10)
•
giving it a title if it is a more artistic piece and if there is a story behind it.
•
display many like objects together
•
provide white space around expensive “art” objects (the more space it is given, the more people perceive
it to be worth)
•
display work at different heights, using clear plastic risers
•
keep your display clean and simple: don’t overwhelm with too much
On pricing, Laura recommends checking out the competition. To start, pick a price in the mid range, or perhaps a
little lower. You can always raise your prices. Customers of yours will feel good about their wise, early purchase
when your prices go up, but nobody feels good if your prices go down.
On trends, high end sales are dropping as we are seeing fewer rich American tourists. However, the local market
for functional wood objects is getting hotter. The Olympics in 2010 will obviously affect the market. 2009 is also
expected to be a good year for tourism and many arts events are being planned to take advantage of the expected
influx of tourists.
Our thanks to Laura for giving us an insiders view on a topic many of us know little about.

RICHMOND CARVER’S SHOW – Thanks a Bunch!

Another of the club’s civic activities has passed into

our club members. I would like to personally acknowledge and thank Marco Berera, Allan Cusworth, Frank Cullis, Ted Fromson, Steve Hansen,

RUSS FAIRFIELD DEMO AND CLASSES
Art Liestman
We are happy to inform you
that Russ Fairfield, from Post
Falls, Idaho, will be here on
Saturday, September 10th for a
lecture/demo and for handson classes on September 11th
and 12th (if there is enough
demand). Russ is an experienced woodturner and an excellent demonstrator. Longtime members will recall that
Russ did a joint demonstration for the GVWG and the
Fraser Valley Woodturners a
few years ago and kept everyone’s attention for the full two
days. We’re very excited to
be bringing him back!
Russ credits a hurricane as the
reason for his devotion to
woodturning. For several
years, Russ made replica tall clocks as a hobby and part-time job. The wood lathe was a part of his home-shop for
making finials and other parts for these clocks, pianos, and furniture. But, he had never made a bowl or other
form. All of that changed when
Russ had a chance meeting with
Melvin Lindquist and John Read
over a giant Magnolia that had
fallen in Tallahassee, Florida during the hurricane season of 1984.
They awakened him to the many
possibilities of the “art” of turned
wood. He bought a General 260
lathe, added riser blocks to it, and
got seriously into woodturning.
He hasn’t stopped since.
After several years in the southeastern US, Russ moved back
home to Washington state in 1999.
In early 2002, he and his wife
moved to Post Falls, Idaho, where
he has a new shop with enough
space to continue collecting tools
and turning wood for a lot of
years. The past two years have
been busy for Russ with demonstrations for club meetings and
regional symposiums in New
York, Kentucky, Tennessee, North
Carolina, Georgia, Florida, and

Nevada. He has published feature articles on the techniques of turning and finishing in American Woodturner
and in several other woodturning magazines. Russ is an
active participant in the online woodturning site Wood
Central (http://www.woodcentral.com) where many of
his articles have been archived as “Russ’s Corner”. If
you’d like to know more about Russ, see his website at:
http://www.woodturnerruss.com.
On Saturday, September 10th, Russ’s demo will be held
at the Sapperton Pensioners Hall from 9:30 am to approximately 4pm. There is a $25 charge to attend the
demo. The demonstration will focus on spindle turning
(including weed-pots, candle sticks, walking sticks,
pens, and furniture parts) and then on finishing what he
makes.
Russ will teach a hands-on class on Sunday, September
11th and (if there is enough demand) on Monday, September 11th at Island Woodcraft in Coquitlam from 9:30
am to approximately 4pm. When asked what the class
would consist of, Russ responded:
“We often think about spindle turning as beads
and coves on table legs and chair parts. While
these are the basic forms of the spindle, this art
form is really about anything that can be turned
between two centers - pen, weed-pot, candle sticks, walking cane, Christmas ornaments, or the delicate finial on a lidded box. We will explore these spindle forms, and the tools and techniques we
can use to make them. Bring your roughing gouge, parting tool, 1/2” spindle gouge, a 3/4” wide
scraper, and a couple old screwdrivers to the class. We will learn to grind them and use them to
practice the basic cuts used for all spindle turnings. Then, you can use the lathe to follow whatever form of the spindle you may wish to explore. Notice that a skew chisel is
not included. Learning to use a skew chisel is not a prerequisite to turning a spindle.
Why the screwdrivers? We will use them to make our own tools for turning small beads
and captured rings.”
As you can see, the class will be
packed full of information. The
class fee will be $150. We will
have a signup sheet for the class
at the June meeting. We need to
get an idea of whether there will
be enough demand for two class
days, so please give it some
thought.
RUSS FAIRFIELD DEMO AND CLASSES (Cont.)

TIPS, TRICKS AND PROBLEMS
Submitted by Kerry Deane Cloutier
Like many of us, I use tung oil when I want a semi-gloss finish. However, I have had some problems when finishing items with small voids or holes, such as Ambrosia Maple. I find that the finish bubbles out of the holes after
the excess oil has been wiped off, leaving a bump or pool on the surface. I have tried re-wiping the piece when I
noticed the pool, but that mars the finish. I have tried using compressed air to blow out the holes, but that seemed
to have no effect.
Any suggestions?
Email Kerry at kerry@runningdogwoodworking.com & we’ll include them in the next newsletter.

COMING EVENTS
SUPPORT YOUR ART/CRAFT – COLLECT
Bruce Campbell
One of the very best parts of our Guild is the positive impact it has had on the work of our members. Speaking for
myself, I get something from every Guild event whether it is information on a tool, a new technique, or an idea for
a new piece. Others must be having the same experience because many of you, regardless of your current skill, are
making significant improvements in the quality, complexity and variety of your work.
Several years ago I learned there is a downside to this. One of our members produces a series of work that I really
like but he has become well enough established that I can’t afford his work any more. So I decided to start collecting early. That is, early in the career of turners whose work I like. When I see a piece that I like I offer to buy it
outright or trade for something that I have turned. It is a complicated process because some have not thought about
selling their work or what they want for it. But it is also really rewarding because of the encouragement that it
gives people and the fun we have deciding on a reasonable “deal”.
In many cases I can “copy” the work but somehow it is not the same. It lacks the relationship that is established by
getting it from the one who made it. So I encourage you all to start collecting. It need not cost a lot of money but
it will make a significant difference to you and the turners you choose to support.
